extracted.intended_audience: practitioners before the USPTO (patent attorneys/agents), OED staff, and administrative law practitioners handling USPTO disciplinary matters
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, procedural rules, burdens, and sanctioning factors applied in USPTO Office of Enrollment and Discipline proceedings for practitioners accused of ethical or professional misconduct before the USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO authority to suspend or exclude practitioners (35 U.S.C. § 32)
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO has the 'exclusive authority to establish qualifications for admitting persons to practice before it, and to suspend or exclude them from practicing before it.' The Director of the USPTO may suspend or exclude a person from practice if the person is 'shown to be incompetent or disreputable, or guilty of gross misconduct,' or if the person violates regulations established by the Office. 35 U.S.C. § 32.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the statutory basis for OED proceedings and sanctions; violations of USPTO regulations or evidence of incompetence/disreputability can support suspension or exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on disreputable or gross misconduct (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursuant to USPTO regulation 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a), practitioners shall not 'engage in disreputable or gross misconduct.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State disciplinary suspensions imposed on ethical grounds are treated as conduct violating § 10.23(a). The regulation provides a basis to sanction practitioners for ethical failures even when the conduct originated outside USPTO proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners shall not 'engage in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice.' 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An attorney's failure to cooperate with disciplinary investigations is an independent act of misconduct falling under this subsection; conduct that negatively impacts the public's perception or efficacy of the courts or legal profession qualifies. Case law examples cited: Attorney Grievance Comm'n v. Rand; Iowa Supreme Court Attorney Disciplinary Bd. v. Marks; Disciplinary Counsel v. Wolanin; In re Netusil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catch‑all prohibition on conduct reflecting adversely on fitness (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not 'engage in any other conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner's fitness to practice before the Office.' 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This subsection is a catch‑all for conduct not covered by (b)(1)–(b)(5). If alleged conduct violates any provision of § 10.23(b)(1)–(5), it cannot also be charged under (b)(6) for the same conduct. Precedent: In re Lane; In re Kelber. The OED must allege distinct misconduct to prove a (b)(6) violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: State bar suspension as grounds for USPTO misconduct (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(5) interplay)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspension from practice as an attorney on ethical grounds by a state bar is considered conduct constituting a violation of paragraphs (a) and (b) of 37 C.F.R. § 10.23 (via § 10.23(c)(5)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practitioner’s suspension by a state court for ethical reasons can be used as evidence of misconduct before the USPTO and support charges under USPTO disciplinary rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to cooperate / knowingly fail to respond to lawful demand (37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct state that practitioners shall not 'fail to cooperate with the [OED] in an investigation of any matter before it, or knowingly fail to respond to a lawful demand or request for information from an admissions or disciplinary authority.' 37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practitioner's knowing failure to respond to an RFI or other lawful demand constitutes professional misconduct. 'Knowingly' means actual knowledge, and knowledge may be inferred from circumstances (37 C.F.R. § 11.1). Repeated failures to respond to RFIs and disciplinary inquiries are aggravating and support findings of misconduct under this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional misconduct / prejudicial conduct under Rules (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(a) and (d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Violation of § 11.801(b) (failure to cooperate) is professional misconduct under 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(a). Such misconduct also constitutes conduct 'that is prejudicial to the administration of justice' under 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A finding that a practitioner failed to cooperate with OED investigations establishes both professional misconduct and a violation for prejudicing the administration of justice; the decision cites prior discussion of how failure-to-cooperate undermines public confidence in self-regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof: clear and convincing evidence (37 C.F.R. § 11.49)
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director has the burden of proving alleged violations by 'clear and convincing evidence.' 37 C.F.R. § 11.49. Thereafter, Respondent has the burden to prove any affirmative defense by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision explains the clear and convincing standard as intermediate between preponderance and beyond a reasonable doubt, citing Addington v. Texas, and provides judicial definitions: evidence that produces 'a firm belief or conviction' and is 'certain, unambiguous, and plain' (Jimenez; Foster). This elevated standard protects important liberty interests in disciplinary contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and application of 'clear and convincing' evidence (case law guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear and convincing evidence requires 'evidence of such weight that it produces in the mind of the trier of fact a firm belief or conviction, without hesitancy, as to the truth of the allegations sought to be established.' (Addington; Jimenez; Foster).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision quotes and applies these definitions to explain why the OED met its burden where the respondent admitted suspensions and failed to rebut evidence of nonresponse to RFIs. Use these definitions when assessing sufficiency of proof in disciplinary matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirmative defenses pleading requirements (37 C.F.R. § 11.36)
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO regulations require Respondent to 'state affirmatively in the answer special matters of defense and any intent to raise a disability as a mitigating factor.' If an affirmative defense is raised, an answer must 'specify the defense or disability, its nexus to the misconduct, and the reason it provides a defense or mitigation.' 37 C.F.R. § 11.36.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely listing legal doctrines without specifying how they relate to the alleged misconduct is insufficient to give fair notice and fails regulatory requirements. The respondent must both plead and prove affirmative defenses with the required specificity and the clear and convincing standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctioning factors (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Before sanctioning a practitioner, the Court must consider the following four factors: (1) Whether the practitioner has violated a duty owed to a Client, to the public, to the legal system, or to the profession; (2) Whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) The amount of the actual or potential injury caused by the practitioner's misconduct; and (4) the existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors. 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four factors form the core of sanction analysis. The decision applies them: finding duties violated (cooperation duty), intent (knowing), little or no actual injury shown, and both aggravating (pattern, deceptive practices) and limited mitigating factors (later reinstatement in state bar).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions in assessing aggravating/mitigating factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court often looks to the ABA's Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions ('ABA Standards') when determining whether aggravating or mitigating factors exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggravating factors recognized include a pattern of misconduct and deceptive practices during the disciplinary process; mitigating factors may include cooperation or rehabilitation, but must be supported by the record. The decision cites case law applying ABA Standards and gives examples of sanctions in analogous cases (e.g., 60‑day suspension; 30‑day suspension with conditions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner duty to maintain current contact information (37 C.F.R. § 11.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must file written notice of any change of address as required by regulations governing recognition of practitioners to practice before the USPTO. 37 C.F.R. § 11.11.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to keep OED apprised of current address or e‑mail can not excuse nonresponse to RFIs and may support findings that the practitioner 'knew' of the RFI (especially when RFI was also e‑mailed to an address previously provided). Misstating address may be considered deceptive and be aggravating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge may be inferred from circumstances (37 C.F.R. § 11.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'knowingly' means actual knowledge of the fact in question, and a person's knowledge may be inferred from the circumstances. 37 C.F.R. § 11.1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a respondent had contact with OED or provided an e‑mail address that received RFIs, the court may infer actual knowledge even if the respondent claims otherwise; this inference supports findings of knowing failure to respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural / remedial rules: duties while suspended, reinstatement, and appeal rights (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.58, 11.60(c), 11.55(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations set forth respondent's duties while suspended (37 C.F.R. § 11.58), the process for petitioning for reinstatement (37 C.F.R. § 11.60(c)), and appeal rights to the USPTO Director within 30 days (37 C.F.R. § 11.55(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanctions orders should reference these provisions to notify practitioners of obligations during suspension, the mechanism and standard for seeking reinstatement, and the timeline for appeals. The decision orders suspension with most of it stayed, probation, and directs respondent to the cited sections for duties and reinstatement procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural expectations in OED proceedings (notice, hearing appearance, post‑hearing briefs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties are entitled to notice of hearing (e.g., Notice of Hearing and Order advising time, date, location), and the parties were afforded opportunity to file post‑hearing briefs and response briefs within specified deadlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to appear at the hearing, failure to notify the court, and failure to file post‑hearing briefs forfeits opportunity to present evidence and can lead the tribunal to deem unchallenged allegations admitted or sufficiently proven. Service by mail and e‑mail that is not returned as undeliverable is evidence of proper notice.
